The most fundamental flaw of capitalism

Interesting. I would like to point out though that he doesn't take into consideration the human factor of why we have bosses and single points of decision making rather than decision making by committee. Decisions by committee are not always "everyone agrees and everything is happy and okay." Often times committees are much slower at decision making (everyone has to have a say) and can cause tension among a group because people will tend to faction off into sub-groups because we don't all think alike. And that's not to say committees don't work in all circumstances but running a restaurant by committee could cause a lot of tension. I don't like blue, but the others liked blue so now the interior design is blue focused. Now because I had the opportunity to help the committee decide and failed I have to live with the fact that not only do I not like the restaurant design, but now I know my fellow coworkers don't like my ideas. Where as if it was just a boss deciding the color I wouldn't have that second resentment or tension with my fellow committee members. This can be applied to any decisions I just used the color as an easy example.

The simple fact is that we are NOT all equal in terms of intelligence. Some people, like it or not, are more intelligent and better at making decisions, motivating a workforce, or designing processes to be the most efficient. Title pretty much says it all. I'm tired of hearing about something that I know basically nothing about, so it's time to start doing some research. My question is, where should I start? Thanks in advance.
What do I need to read to understand global warming/climate change?

If you want a full understanding of climate change you need to study the field of Climate Dynamics. This link is to a six chapter book that is a great place to start. You do need a basic understanding of Calculus and differential equations to understand the mathematics; however, it is worth skimming through even if you do not have the needed math background.

Other than finding textbooks that cover how we model the climate, you can start reading the huge amount of research on the subject. Most research is extremely complicated. You can always find reviews of an article, to supplement your studies, especially if the article is too complex on your first reading. JSTOR.org and arXiv.org are two of the more popular online databases. On arXiv it is likely you will find more mathematically complex articles than elsewhere on the web. I'm sure there are specific journals that publish only material on climate change but I am not sure of their names.

I've just begun reading your first link (and I apologize if the answer I'm seeking is covered in it) but I'm reminded of an argument against current climate models which contests the inclusion of H2O as an aerosol (at least in regards to the way it traps heat.) The opponents state that H2O does not in fact deflect heat back downward, or at least not to the degree claimed by current models. Is this a common argument that I can have squashed here and now, and get on with my research? Or is this actually a contested point?

Thanks!

I found a reading list on NPR's website. It's a few years old, but might be helpful.

http://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=121057831

Edit: Unless you are an academic yourself (in which case you probably wouldn't be asking this question here..) I wouldn't bother with the actual peer-reviewed literature. It's written by and to people who are already experts. You're only going to get frustrated.

Green house gases and how they operate(What they are, how they work, how they're distributed) weather patterns and oscillations through history(You'll be able to find the data on this with enough searching) and try to understand how scientists determine the historical temperatures as well and how they determine historical green house gas emissions. After that it shouldn't be too hard to understand the consensus around climate change, how its changing. However to understand how increasing temperatures impact the climate you'll have to search deeper as that modeling is a bitch and a half.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming

It's rather quite simple: release more CO2 (which has a higher heat capacity and absorbs more infrared (heat) radiation than oxygen), and the earth will retain more heat, and become warmer.

Assuming you want to understand the mechanisms and be able to intelligently assess arguments, you need an undergraduate level understanding of quantum chemistry. Assuming you want to understand and assess the evidence, you need a similar level of understanding of statistics.
